audience: Travellers, seven in ten of them American, who are planning a stay in Sicily: couples, families, small groups and guests of villas who pay 100 to 200 EUR per person for a private experience with a chef in Palermo, a hands-on class in his kitchen or a dinner cooked and served where they stay. They meet the house while they dream of the trip, save it while they plan, and write when they want to book. They compare RistHome with starred restaurants and five-star hotels, not with caterers.
voice: Write as the house, in the first person plural or with no subject at all. Calm, exact, warm. Never as a salesman.
Say less. One idea per post, one thought per text. An empty text is better than a filler line: the photo speaks alone.
Name things the way these houses do: the dish by the chef's own name, then at most two elements, ingredient and method or origin ("red prawn, simply grilled"). No adjectives of taste, no praise.

Name a dish only with the CHEF'S NAME given next to its photo. Without one, never describe the food by shape, colour, container or material: leave the text empty, or write a short line about the moment of the experience that the brand facts support (the chef's kitchen, cooking side by side, the table being laid, service at your home).
Concrete nouns over adjectives: place (Palermo, the chef's kitchen), people (Chef Giacomo Napolitano), gesture (rolled by hand, plated at your table) when the photo shows it.
The hook promises the experience and the guest's place in it, not a list of items and not a question.
One invitation at the end, phrased as a host would: the exact CTA line given, once. Nothing else asks for anything.
Never ask for engagement: no "comment", "tag a friend", "share", "follow us", "save this post", no questions to the reader. The house keeps a courteous distance.
Proof is stated once, flat, as a fact (the Google rating or the chef's background), never as a boast.
American English, in spelling and in idiom.
The cover line gives a feeling the traveller wants, never the name of a service: two short sentences at most, ten words in all. ("You came to Sicily for the food. Make it personal.")
The experience leads, the dish follows: the place, the hands, the table and the moment it is served say more than a finished plate alone.
Never claim luxury: no hype words, no superlatives, no exclamation marks, no urgency, no prices, no discounts.
No words on a slide twice: a line said on the cover is not said again on the next slide, and no two slides carry the same sentence.

A dish is named only in the chef's own words, as its main ingredients separated by commas. Without them the slide carries no title: never a bare course name (Primo, Antipasto, Dolce), which a traveller does not read as a dish.
Plain American English that a person would say aloud: "at your villa", "at your table", "in your kitchen". Never constructions that only sound written ("where you stay", "laid where you stay").
The caption is set like a short page: three to five short paragraphs with a blank line between them; the first is the promise, the last is the invitation.
Two to four small symbols may mark the lines of a caption (the place, the season, the table); never in a row, never as decoration at the end, never on a slide.
visual: One subject per frame, with air around it, and few colours. Crowded trays, buffet overviews and repeated identical items read as catering, not as a private table.
Prefer, in this order: the chef's hands touching the food (kneading, plating, pouring), a single plated dish, raw produce, the laid table and its setting, the chef. Finished buffets come last.
Natural or warm low light, true colours. No flash glare, no blown highlights, no mixed colour casts.
Clean surfaces: no plastic, no disposable containers, no packaging, no clutter, no phone-screen artefacts.
The first frame is the strongest picture of the post; the last picture before the invitation is the served dish or the laid table.
structure: Open on the single most beautiful image (people decide in the first second and judge the whole by its opening).
Follow the order of the real experience: produce, gesture, plate, table. A sequence the viewer can predict feels effortless.
End on the peak: the served dish or the table, then one quiet invitation.
Slow, even pacing. Fewer, longer scenes rather than many fast cuts.
Repeat the same few signature elements in every post (wordmark, type, tone) so the house is recognised without reading.
Every piece is something a traveller would send to the person they are travelling with: one clear promise of an experience in Sicily, readable without knowing the house.
Sicily or Palermo is named on the first or the second slide; the service (private chef, cooking class) is named in the cover's small line.

rules: The house sells two private experiences only: the cooking class and the chef at home. Nothing else enters the calendar.
A week reads like a tasting menu: no format twice in a row, the two experiences alternate, each post stands on its own.
A day without a post is better than a post below the standard: when the material is not good enough the slot stays empty.
At most one post in seven asks for a booking outright; the others show the craft and let the single closing line invite.
Same hour every time, so the house is expected and never intrudes.
Seasons and produce set the themes. No trends, no memes, no borrowed holidays, no reactions to other accounts.
Every post is written in English: the guests come from abroad.
Four posts a week, on the same days: the island, the craft, the table, the season. Dishes are one voice among four; the place, the produce and the hands carry the others.
A piece about the island or the season may open on a licensed photograph of Sicily, credited, and always ends on the house's own table or dish.

carousel: A photograph large enough to stay sharp fills the slide, like the cover, with its few words low on the picture; a smaller one sits whole on the cream mat. Same margins, same type, the wordmark small and always in the same place.
One serif for the words and one small sans for the marks; four type styles in all. Hierarchy comes from empty space, not from size.
Neutrals only: the photograph supplies the colour.
Capitals on one line at most, letterspaced; lowercase is never letterspaced; text is ragged, never justified.
The first slide sets the ratio of all the others; what matters stays inside the centre square the profile grid shows.
The second slide must work as a second cover: people who did not swipe are shown the post again from there.
Each photograph has a role of its own in the sequence; none is there only to fill a place.

A closer look may follow the photograph it is cut from, once in a carousel at most: the photograph's own pixels, about half the picture across, never enlarged more than 1.25 times. It never stands in for the whole photograph.
The last slide closes the piece: the wordmark, one invitation, a thin rule.
editing: Allowed on a photograph: crop, straighten, exposure, white balance, the single house colour grade, enlargement that does not invent detail, removal of sensor dust.
Never: adding, removing or rearranging anything in the frame, changing a colour so the dish looks different, generating or regenerating any part of the food, the table, the kitchen or a person.
A still is moved only when the move reveals something; otherwise it is held.
Generated material is context only (the sea, a leaf, the light), never opens or closes a post, and is always disclosed.

principles.rule: Few words, one booking verb, no selling language.
principles.why: The twelve reference houses use very short copy and a single request-style booking line; three take requests only or no bookings.

principles.rule: Never ask for likes, comments, tags or follows.
principles.why: High brand-to-consumer engagement on social media lowers the perceived value of a luxury brand; psychological distance carries the effect.
principles.source: Park, Im & Kim 2020, Journal of Business Research

principles.rule: One subject, few colours, air around it.
principles.why: Visual and colour complexity lower perceived brand status; simple images read as curated.
principles.source: Adam & Wen 2026, JAMS; J. Brand Management 2018

principles.rule: Ingredient and method or origin; no praise words.
principles.why: Expensive menus name provenance far more often; vague praise words track lower prices.
principles.source: Jurafsky, The Language of Food (press coverage)

principles.rule: Show the chef's hand touching the food.
principles.why: A hand touching the product raises the viewer's sense of ownership and valuation; the hand must touch, not merely appear.
principles.source: Luangrath et al. 2022, Journal of Marketing Research

principles.rule: Prefer pictures with implied motion: pouring, steam, a gesture in progress.
principles.why: Implied motion raises the perceived freshness and appeal of food.
principles.source: Gvili et al. 2015, Food Quality and Preference

principles.rule: The food and the craft carry the post, not the decor or the claims.
principles.why: Michelin stars judge ingredient quality, harmony of flavours, mastery of technique, the chef's personality in the cuisine and consistency: the food on the plate, nothing more.
principles.source: MICHELIN Guide, What is a Michelin Star

principles.rule: Same wordmark, type, tone and pacing in every post; never one weak post between two good ones.
principles.why: Consistency across the menu and over time is a star criterion; inspectors return several times.

principles.rule: Speak as a host receiving friends: warm, never intrusive, never pushing.
principles.why: Hospitality as an ethic: guests are greeted as friends and wishes anticipated without intrusion; service weighs most in how a visit is remembered.
principles.source: Relais & Châteaux values; Forbes Travel Guide

principles.rule: Open on the best image; end on the served dish or the laid table.
principles.why: First impressions anchor judgement and experiences are remembered by their peak and their end.
principles.source: established findings in cognitive psychology (primacy effect, peak-end rule); not re-verified in this research

principles.rule: Nothing is shown or named that the guest will not find.
principles.why: Guides visit anonymously and pay in full: the promise is checked against the real table.

rules: The first sentence of every caption says what the house is and where, in the words people type when they search: private chef or cooking class, Palermo, Sicily.
One subject per post, named once in plain words; no keyword lists, no repeated phrases.
Three to five hashtags, always the place and the house, then the service. Never trend tags.
Every image carries a description of what it shows, with the house and the place (alt text): it is read by people who cannot see and by search.
The same name, the same place and the same words on every channel, so the house is found as one thing.

measure.commercial: margin from bookings divided by reach, times 1000 (value per 1,000 reached)
rules: Sends carry a post to people who do not follow the house: they are read before likes.
A post is compared with the account's own median, never with other accounts.
Reach from the United States is noted for every post once the channel reports it.

scorecard.note: An editorial judgement on a finished piece, not a forecast of reach. Below the threshold the piece is revised or the slot stays empty. The hard gates stand apart from the score.

criteria.label: Hook and stopping power
criteria.asks: Would a traveller planning Sicily stop on the first picture and its line within a second, without knowing the house?

criteria.label: Visual and editorial quality
criteria.asks: Does every picture look chosen and composed: one subject, air, true colour, the house's own system?

criteria.label: Narrative strength
criteria.asks: Does the sequence follow the real experience and end on its peak, each picture with a role of its own?

criteria.label: Relevance to the American traveller
criteria.asks: Does it answer what someone planning a stay in Sicily wants to feel and to know, in American English?

criteria.label: Sending and discovery
criteria.asks: Is there a reason to send it to the person one is travelling with, earned by the piece and never asked for? Is it findable by place and service?

criteria.label: Coherence with the house
criteria.asks: Wordmark, type, tone and restraint as in every other piece?

criteria.label: Clarity of the invitation
criteria.asks: Is it plain what the experience is, where it happens and how to ask for availability, with one invitation only?

hardGates.asks: The deterministic gate passes: limits, vocabulary, place, calendar.
Every claim is in content/brand-facts.json or visible in the photograph.
Nothing generated or borrowed is shown as the house's own table, dish, kitchen, chef or guests.
No recognisable guest without recorded consent; every licensed picture is credited.
